P.title: P.blurb
Art & Culture: Painting, music, literature, cinema and architecture.

P.title: ar-painting.summary
Art & Culture: From the Renaissance to modern art.

P.title: ar-painting.q0.q
Art & Culture: Which movement captured light with quick outdoor brushstrokes?

P.title: ar-painting.q0.x
Art & Culture: Monet's "Impression, Sunrise" gave it its name.

P.title: ar-painting.q2.q
Art & Culture: Which technique creates depth with lines meeting at a point?

P.title: ar-painting.c0.text
Art & Culture: In 15th–16th century Italy, artists revived ancient Greek and Roman ideas and studied anatomy and perspective. Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael are its giants.

P.title: ar-painting.c1.text
Art & Culture: Renaissance painters used vanishing points: parallel lines converge to a point on the horizon, creating the illusion of depth on a flat surface.

P.title: ar-painting.c2.text
Art & Culture: In the 1600s, Baroque art went for drama: strong light and dark (chiaroscuro), movement and emotion. Caravaggio, Rembrandt and Velázquez led the way.

P.title: ar-painting.c3.text
Art & Culture: In 1870s Paris, Monet, Renoir and Degas painted outdoors with quick brushstrokes, capturing light and moments rather than fine detail. The name started as an insult.

P.title: ar-painting.c4.text
Art & Culture: Van Gogh, Cézanne and Gauguin pushed further: bold colours, expressive brushwork and simplified shapes. Van Gogh sold very few paintings in his lifetime.

P.title: ar-painting.c5.text
Art & Culture: Picasso and Braque broke objects into geometric shapes and showed several viewpoints at once. *Les Demoiselles d'Avignon* (1907) shocked even their friends.

P.title: ar-painting.c6.text
Art & Culture: Surrealists like Dalí and Magritte painted dreams and the unconscious, inspired by Freud. Melting clocks and pipes that "are not a pipe" made viewers question reality.

P.title: ar-painting.c7.text
Art & Culture: Kandinsky and Mondrian made art that didn't depict anything recognisable: just colour, line and form. Later, Jackson Pollock dripped paint across canvases on the floor.

P.title: ar-painting.c8.text
Art & Culture: In the 1960s, Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein turned soup cans, celebrities and comics into art, blurring the line between art and advertising.

P.title: ar-painting.c9.text
Art & Culture: Portugal's art includes Nuno Gonçalves' 15th-century *Saint Vincent Panels*, Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso's modernism and Paula Rego's powerful storytelling.

P.title: ar-music.q0.q
Art & Culture: What is the frequency of concert A?

P.title: ar-music.q1.q
Art & Culture: Which notes make a C major chord?

P.title: ar-music.c0.text
Art & Culture: A note's pitch is its frequency: how many vibrations per second. The A above middle C is usually tuned to 440 Hz.

P.title: ar-music.c1.text
Art & Culture: Doubling a frequency gives the same note an octave higher. Western music divides the octave into 12 semitones, the white and black keys of a piano.

P.title: ar-music.c2.text
Art & Culture: A major scale follows a pattern of whole and half steps. Major tends to sound bright; minor tends to sound sadder.

P.title: ar-music.c3.text
Art & Culture: A chord is notes played together. A major chord stacks a root, a major third and a fifth; C major is C, E and G.

P.title: ar-music.c4.text
Art & Culture: A huge number of pop songs use the same four chords, often I–V–vi–IV. In C major that's C, G, Am and F.

P.title: ar-music.c5.text
Art & Culture: Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds; tempo is the speed, measured in beats per minute. Most pop sits around 100–130 BPM.

P.title: ar-music.c6.text
Art & Culture: Orchestras group instruments by how they make sound: strings, woodwind, brass and percussion.

P.title: ar-music.c7.text
Art & Culture: Western classical music is often split into eras: Baroque (Bach), Classical (Mozart), Romantic (Beethoven to Tchaikovsky) and modern.

P.title: ar-music.c8.text
Art & Culture: Fado, born in Lisbon in the early 1800s, is sung with Portuguese guitar and classical guitar and expresses *saudade*. Amália Rodrigues made it world famous. It's UNESCO-listed since 2011.

P.title: ar-music.c9.text
Art & Culture: Music triggers dopamine, especially just before an expected peak. Surprise and resolution, tension and release, are what give us chills.

P.title: ar-books.q0.q
Art & Culture: Which Portuguese writer won the Nobel Prize in 1998?

P.title: ar-books.q1.o1
Art & Culture: Vasco da Gama's voyage and Portuguese history

P.title: ar-books.c0.text
Art & Culture: The *Epic of Gilgamesh*, from ancient Mesopotamia, is one of the oldest surviving stories, more than 4,000 years old. It's about friendship, loss and the search for immortality.

P.title: ar-books.c1.text
Art & Culture: The *Iliad* tells of the Trojan War; the *Odyssey* follows Odysseus' 10-year journey home. Both were probably composed orally before being written down.

P.title: ar-books.c2.text
Art & Culture: Joseph Campbell found a common pattern in myths: a hero leaves home, faces trials, wins a prize and returns changed. *Star Wars* used it on purpose.

P.title: ar-books.c3.text
Art & Culture: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) wrote around 39 plays and 154 sonnets, and gave English hundreds of words and phrases, like "break the ice".

P.title: ar-books.c3.viz.items.2.l
Art & Culture: words first recorded in his work

P.title: ar-books.c4.text
Art & Culture: Luís de Camões' epic poem (1572) celebrates Vasco da Gama's voyage to India and Portuguese history. 10 June, Portugal's national day, marks Camões' death.

P.title: ar-books.c5.text
Art & Culture: The novel grew in the 17th–18th centuries. *Don Quixote* (1605) is often called the first modern novel; the 19th century brought Austen, Dickens, Tolstoy and Eça de Queirós.

P.title: ar-books.c6.text
Art & Culture: José Saramago won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998, the first writer in Portuguese to do so. His novels, like *Blindness*, use long sentences with little punctuation.

P.title: ar-books.c7.text
Art & Culture: Literature has families: tragedy and comedy from the Greeks, plus poetry, novels, science fiction, crime, fantasy and more. Many books mix them.

P.title: ar-books.c8.text
Art & Culture: Writers make readers feel by showing actions and details rather than stating emotions directly.

P.title: ar-books.c8.viz.items.0.r
Art & Culture: She checked her phone for the third time in a minute

P.title: ar-books.c9.text
Art & Culture: Studies suggest reading fiction may improve our ability to understand others' feelings, by practising seeing through someone else's eyes.

P.title: ar-film.summary
Art & Culture: How moving pictures work and changed the world.

P.title: ar-film.q0.q
Art & Culture: How many frames per second does film usually use?

P.title: ar-film.q1.q
Art & Culture: What did the Kuleshov effect show?

P.title: ar-film.q1.o1
Art & Culture: Editing changes how we read a face

P.title: ar-film.c0.text
Art & Culture: Film is a series of still images shown quickly, usually 24 frames per second. The brain blends them into smooth motion.

P.title: ar-film.c1.text
Art & Culture: In 1895 the Lumière brothers showed short films to a paying audience in Paris. Georges Méliès soon invented special effects with *A Trip to the Moon* (1902).

P.title: ar-film.c2.text
Art & Culture: *The Jazz Singer* (1927) brought synchronised dialogue. Many silent stars, like Charlie Chaplin, struggled or resisted at first.

P.title: ar-film.c3.text
Art & Culture: Shot size tells you what to feel. Wide shots show place and scale; close-ups show emotion; over-the-shoulder shots put you in a conversation.

P.title: ar-film.c4.text
Art & Culture: Editing is invisible storytelling. The Kuleshov effect showed that the same neutral face seems hungry, sad or loving depending on the shot that follows it.

P.title: ar-film.c5.text
Art & Culture: Most films follow three acts: set-up, confrontation and resolution, with turning points between them.

P.title: ar-film.c6.text
Art & Culture: Music guides emotion. Two notes from *Jaws* or the opening of *Star Wars* can make you feel something before you see anything.

P.title: ar-film.c7.text
Art & Culture: Animation creates motion frame by frame, by hand, stop-motion or computer. *Toy Story* (1995) was the first fully computer-animated feature film.

P.title: ar-film.c8.text
Art & Culture: Manoel de Oliveira directed films for over 80 years, until he was over 100. Directors like João César Monteiro and Pedro Costa won prizes abroad.

P.title: ar-film.c9.text
Art & Culture: Next time you watch a film, notice: how long the shots last, when the music starts, and where the camera is when a character makes a big decision.

P.title: ar-arch.summary
Art & Culture: Buildings, styles and the art of everyday things.

P.title: ar-arch.q0.q
Art & Culture: Which style is Portugal's own, seen in the Jerónimos Monastery?

P.title: ar-arch.q1.q
Art & Culture: Which Portuguese architects won the Pritzker Prize?

P.title: ar-arch.q1.x
Art & Culture: Álvaro Siza (1992) and Eduardo Souto de Moura (2011).

P.title: ar-arch.c0.text
Art & Culture: Greek and Roman architecture used column styles called orders: Doric (simple), Ionic (scrolls) and Corinthian (leaves).

P.title: ar-arch.c1.text
Art & Culture: Romans perfected the arch, which turns a load into sideways forces carried down to the ground. With concrete, they built the Pantheon dome, still unreinforced and standing.

P.title: ar-arch.c2.text
Art & Culture: Gothic cathedrals (12th–16th centuries) used pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses to build higher walls full of stained glass.

P.title: ar-arch.c3.text
Art & Culture: Portugal's own late-Gothic style, named after King Manuel I, decorates buildings with ropes, shells, armillary spheres and sea motifs. See the Jerónimos Monastery and Belém Tower.

P.title: ar-arch.c4.text
Art & Culture: Portugal's painted tiles, inspired by Moorish designs, cover churches, stations and houses. The blue-and-white style became popular in the 17th–18th centuries.

P.title: ar-arch.c5.text
Art & Culture: After the 1755 earthquake, Lisbon's Baixa was rebuilt on a grid with the "gaiola pombalina", a wooden frame designed to flex in earthquakes: one of the first anti-seismic designs.

P.title: ar-arch.c6.text
Art & Culture: Modernist architects argued buildings should be shaped by what they do, not decoration. Le Corbusier called a house "a machine for living in".

P.title: ar-arch.c7.text
Art & Culture: Portuguese architects Álvaro Siza (1992) and Eduardo Souto de Moura (2011) both won the Pritzker Prize, architecture's top honour.

P.title: ar-arch.c7.viz.events.2.l
Art & Culture: Souto de Moura wins the Pritzker

P.title: ar-arch.c8.text
Art & Culture: Designer Dieter Rams proposed principles of good design, including: useful, understandable, honest, long-lasting and "as little design as possible".

P.title: ar-arch.c9.text
Art & Culture: The golden ratio (about 1.618) appears in maths and some art, but many claims, like the Parthenon or the Mona Lisa being built on it, are unproven.

P.title: ar-arch.c9.viz.items.0.w
Art & Culture: The Parthenon is built on the golden ratio

P.title: ar-arch.c9.viz.items.0.r
Art & Culture: An appealing story without solid evidence

P.title: ar-masters.q1.q
Art & Culture: What did Michelangelo consider himself first?

P.title: ar-masters.q2.q
Art & Culture: Who painted the School of Athens?

P.title: ar-masters.q2.x
Art & Culture: Plato and Aristotle at the centre.

P.title: ar-masters.c0.text
Art & Culture: Leonardo (1452–1519) was painter, engineer, anatomist and inventor. Only around 15–20 paintings are firmly attributed to him, but his notebooks fill thousands of pages.

P.title: ar-masters.c1.text
Art & Culture: Painted from about 1503, the Mona Lisa's fame comes from its soft blending (sfumato), mysterious smile and a 1911 theft that made headlines worldwide.

P.title: ar-masters.c2.text
Art & Culture: Leonardo blended colours and tones so softly that edges seem to dissolve, like smoke. It gives faces life and mystery.

P.title: ar-masters.c3.text
Art & Culture: Leonardo's mural in Milan captures the moment Jesus says one apostle will betray him. He experimented with paint on dry plaster, so it began flaking within decades.

P.title: ar-masters.c4.text
Art & Culture: Michelangelo (1475–1564) saw himself as a sculptor first. He carved David from a single block of marble in his twenties.

P.title: ar-masters.c5.text
Art & Culture: Michelangelo painted over 300 figures on the Sistine Chapel ceiling in about four years, standing on scaffolding and craning his neck, not lying on his back.

P.title: ar-masters.c6.text
Art & Culture: Raphael (1483–1520) was famous for harmony and grace. His *School of Athens* gathers ancient philosophers, with Plato and Aristotle at the centre.

P.title: ar-masters.c7.text
Art & Culture: Renaissance art was paid for by wealthy patrons: the Medici in Florence, popes in Rome and guilds. Contracts often specified colours and figures.

P.title: ar-masters.c8.text
Art & Culture: North of the Alps, artists like Jan van Eyck and Albrecht Dürer perfected oil paint and astonishing detail.

P.title: ar-masters.c9.text
Art & Culture: Leonardo and Michelangelo were rivals, once painting opposite walls of the same hall in Florence. Neither finished.

P.title: ar-sculpture.q0.x
Art & Culture: Wax melted out, bronze poured in.

P.title: ar-sculpture.q1.q
Art & Culture: What colour were ancient Greek statues originally?

P.title: ar-sculpture.c0.text
Art & Culture: Sculptors either carve away material, like stone or wood, or build it up by modelling clay or wax, often later cast in bronze.

P.title: ar-sculpture.c1.text
Art & Culture: To cast bronze, a wax model is covered in clay, heated so the wax melts out, and molten bronze is poured into the space.

P.title: ar-sculpture.c2.text
Art & Culture: Greek sculptors moved from stiff figures to natural poses. Contrapposto, weight on one leg, made statues look alive.

P.title: ar-sculpture.c3.text
Art & Culture: Ancient statues weren't pure white: they were brightly painted. The paint wore off over centuries; traces are found with UV light.

P.title: ar-sculpture.c4.text
Art & Culture: Gian Lorenzo Bernini made marble seem soft as flesh. In *The Rape of Proserpina*, Pluto's fingers press into her thigh.

P.title: ar-sculpture.c5.text
Art & Culture: Auguste Rodin's *The Thinker* (1880) began as part of a huge door, *The Gates of Hell*, representing Dante.

P.title: ar-sculpture.c6.text
Art & Culture: In the 20th century, sculptors like Brâncuși, Giacometti and Henry Moore simplified forms, used holes and voids, and explored new materials.

P.title: ar-sculpture.c7.text
Art & Culture: Sculpture shapes cities: monuments, fountains and installations. Lisbon's Padrão dos Descobrimentos (1960) celebrates navigators.

P.title: ar-sculpture.c8.text
Art & Culture: Machado de Castro made Lisbon's equestrian statue of King José I (1775). Contemporary artist Joana Vasconcelos creates monumental works from everyday objects.

P.title: ar-sculpture.c9.text
Art & Culture: Some artists sculpt the landscape itself: Robert Smithson's *Spiral Jetty* (1970) is a coil of rock 460 m long in Utah's Great Salt Lake.

P.title: ar-photo.q0.q
Art & Culture: What are the three parts of the exposure triangle?

P.title: ar-photo.q1.o1
Art & Culture: Just after sunrise and before sunset

P.title: ar-photo.c0.text
Art & Culture: For centuries artists used the camera obscura, a dark room or box with a small hole that projects an upside-down image. Capturing that image permanently came later.

P.title: ar-photo.c1.text
Art & Culture: The oldest surviving photograph from a camera, by Nicéphore Niépce, dates from around 1826–27 and needed hours of exposure. Daguerre's process followed in 1839.

P.title: ar-photo.c2.text
Art & Culture: Three settings control exposure: aperture (how wide the lens opens), shutter speed (how long) and ISO (how sensitive the sensor is).

P.title: ar-photo.c3.text
Art & Culture: Divide the frame into a 3×3 grid and place the subject on a line or intersection. It usually feels more dynamic than dead centre.

P.title: ar-photo.c3.viz.items.0.r
Art & Culture: Place it on a third line

P.title: ar-photo.c4.text
Art & Culture: The hour after sunrise and before sunset gives soft, warm, low light with long shadows, loved by photographers.

P.title: ar-photo.c5.text
Art & Culture: Photographs have shaped history: Capa's war images, the "Napalm Girl" in Vietnam, the "Earthrise" from Apollo 8. A single image can change public opinion.

P.title: ar-photo.c6.text
Art & Culture: Focus on the eyes, use soft side light, shoot at eye level and give people something to do. Candid moments often beat posed ones.

P.title: ar-photo.c7.text
Art & Culture: Phone cameras use computational photography, combining many frames instantly to reduce noise and extend dynamic range. Billions of photos are taken every day.

P.title: ar-photo.c8.text
Art & Culture: For decades critics debated whether photography was art. Today photographers like Cartier-Bresson and Annie Leibovitz are in major museums.

P.title: ar-photo.c9.text
Art & Culture: Photos were edited long before Photoshop, like Stalin removing purged officials. Today AI makes convincing fakes easy, so provenance matters.

P.title: ar-asia.summary
Art & Culture: Ink and brush, woodblock prints, temples, miniatures, geometry and the porcelain that crossed the world.

P.title: ar-asia.q0.x
Art & Culture: The pleasure districts and fashions of Edo.

P.title: ar-asia.q1.q
Art & Culture: Which painter copied prints by Hiroshige in oil paint?

P.title: ar-asia.q2.x
Art & Culture: Built in the 1100s for the god Vishnu.

P.title: ar-asia.q3.q
Art & Culture: What gives celadon its green colour?

P.title: ar-asia.q3.x
Art & Culture: Iron in the glaze turns green in a low-oxygen kiln.

P.title: ar-asia.q4.q
Art & Culture: Where did the cobalt for early blue-and-white porcelain come from?

P.title: ar-asia.q4.x
Art & Culture: It was imported into China in the 1300s.

P.title: ar-asia.c0.text
Art & Culture: In China, beautiful handwriting was long considered the highest of the arts, above painting. A single brushstroke was thought to reveal the writer's character.\n\nCalligraphers used the "four treasures of the study": brush, ink stick, ink stone and paper. Ink cannot be erased, so every stroke has to be right the first time.

P.title: ar-asia.c1.text
Art & Culture: Chinese painters called landscape shanshui, "mountains and water". From the Song dynasty onward it became the most prestigious subject of painting.\n\nPainters used black ink in many shades, and left empty space for mist, water and sky. Scrolls were meant to be read slowly, like a journey through the hills.

P.title: ar-asia.c2.text
Art & Culture: Ukiyo-e means "pictures of the floating world": the pleasure districts, theatres and fashions of Edo, today's Tokyo, from the 1600s to the 1800s.\n\nMost were colour woodblock prints, sold cheaply to ordinary townspeople. Their stars included Utamaro, Hokusai and Hiroshige, whose views of Mount Fuji and the Tōkaidō road became best-sellers.

P.title: ar-asia.c3.text
Art & Culture: When Japan opened to Western trade in the 1850s, its prints flooded into Europe. Hokusai's *Great Wave* and Hiroshige's views struck Paris artists as something completely new.\n\nMonet, Degas, Van Gogh and Mary Cassatt borrowed flat colour, bold outlines, off-centre views and everyday subjects. The craze was called japonisme.

P.title: ar-asia.c4.text
Art & Culture: Hindu temples in India were designed as homes for the gods and models of the cosmos, their towers rising like the sacred mountain at the centre of the world.\n\nTheir walls are covered with sculpture: gods, dancers, animals, lovers and scenes from epic stories. At Ellora, a whole temple was carved downwards out of a single cliff.

P.title: ar-asia.c5.text
Art & Culture: The Mughal emperors, who ruled much of South Asia from 1526, ran royal workshops that produced exquisite small paintings for books and albums.\n\nPersian and Indian artists worked side by side, and later borrowed ideas from European prints. The results include court histories, portraits and astonishingly precise studies of birds, animals and flowers.

P.title: ar-asia.c6.text
Art & Culture: Mosques and many religious buildings avoid pictures of people and animals. Instead, artists developed dazzling ornament from geometry, flowing plant forms and calligraphy.\n\nWith only a compass and a ruler, they built complex star patterns that repeat endlessly across tiles, wood, plaster and metal, from Spain to Central Asia.

P.title: ar-asia.c7.text
Art & Culture: Angkor Wat, in Cambodia, was built in the early 1100s by the Khmer king Suryavarman II as a temple to the Hindu god Vishnu. It later became Buddhist and is still used today.\n\nIt is the largest religious monument in the world. Its five towers stand for the peaks of Mount Meru, home of the gods, and its wide moat for the ocean around it.

P.title: ar-asia.c8.text
Art & Culture: Porcelain is a fine white ceramic made from kaolin clay fired at about 1,300 °C. It is hard, thin and translucent, and for centuries only China knew how to make it.\n\nChinese porcelain was traded across Asia and Africa and, from the 1500s, shipped to Europe in huge quantities. In English it simply became "china".

P.title: ar-asia.c9.text
Art & Culture: During the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392), Korean potters made celadon: stoneware with a soft blue-green glaze admired across East Asia for its jade-like colour.\n\nThey also invented an inlay technique, sanggam: designs were carved into the clay and filled with white and black slip before glazing, giving delicate cranes, clouds and willows.

P.title: ar-asia.c9.viz.steps.1
Art & Culture: Fill with white and black slip

P.title: ar-poetry.q0.q
Art & Culture: How many lines does a sonnet have?

P.title: ar-poetry.q0.x
Art & Culture: Petrarch and Shakespeare used different structures.

P.title: ar-poetry.q2.q
Art & Culture: Which Pessoa book was published in his lifetime?

P.title: ar-poetry.c0.text
Art & Culture: Poetry uses rhythm, sound, imagery and line breaks to compress meaning and feeling. It's meant to be heard as much as read.

P.title: ar-poetry.c1.text
Art & Culture: Metre is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. Shakespeare's iambic pentameter has five da-DUM beats: "shall I com-PARE thee TO a SUM-mer's DAY".

P.title: ar-poetry.c2.text
Art & Culture: A sonnet has 14 lines. Petrarch popularised it in Italy; Shakespeare wrote 154; Camões wrote hundreds of sonnets in Portuguese.

P.title: ar-poetry.c3.text
Art & Culture: The Japanese haiku traditionally has 5–7–5 sound units and captures a moment in nature. Bashō's frog jumping into an old pond is the most famous.

P.title: ar-poetry.c4.text
Art & Culture: A simile compares using "like" or "as"; a metaphor says one thing *is* another. "Life is a journey" shapes how we think about life.

P.title: ar-poetry.c5.text
Art & Culture: Since the late 1800s, many poets abandoned regular rhyme and metre. Walt Whitman's long lines and Pessoa's Álvaro de Campos broke the old rules.

P.title: ar-poetry.c6.text
Art & Culture: Fernando Pessoa's *Mensagem* (1934), the only book in Portuguese he published in his lifetime, reimagines Portuguese history as myth. "O mar salgado, quanto do teu sal / São lágrimas de Portugal!"

P.title: ar-poetry.c7.text
Art & Culture: Florbela Espanca (1894–1930) wrote passionate, intense sonnets about love, longing and identity, and is one of Portugal's most beloved poets.

P.title: ar-poetry.c8.text
Art & Culture: From ancient bards to rap and slam poetry, poetry has always been performed. Rap uses rhyme, rhythm and wordplay as intensely as any sonnet.

P.title: ar-poetry.c9.text
Art & Culture: Read it aloud twice. Notice what surprises you, which images stay with you, where the lines break and what changes by the end.

P.title: ar-theatre.q0.q
Art & Culture: Who is the father of Portuguese theatre?

P.title: ar-theatre.q1.q
Art & Culture: In which city did theatre as we know it begin?

P.title: ar-theatre.c0.text
Art & Culture: Theatre as we know it began in Athens in the 5th century BCE, at festivals for the god Dionysus. Huge open-air theatres seated thousands.

P.title: ar-theatre.c1.text
Art & Culture: Greek tragedy showed noble heroes destroyed by a fatal flaw; comedy mocked politicians and society. The two masks still symbolise theatre.

P.title: ar-theatre.c2.text
Art & Culture: Gil Vicente (c. 1465–1536) is the father of Portuguese theatre. His *Auto da Barca do Inferno* satirises sinners of all classes waiting to board the boats to heaven or hell.

P.title: ar-theatre.c3.text
Art & Culture: Shakespeare's plays were performed at the Globe, an open-air theatre in London where groundlings stood for a penny. All roles were played by men.

P.title: ar-theatre.c4.text
Art & Culture: Italian improvised comedy used stock characters with masks, like Harlequin and Pantalone. It influenced Molière and modern sitcoms.

P.title: ar-theatre.c5.text
Art & Culture: Opera began in Italy around 1600, combining drama, music and spectacle. Lisbon's Teatro Nacional de São Carlos opened in 1793.

P.title: ar-theatre.c6.text
Art & Culture: In the 1800s, Ibsen and Chekhov brought ordinary homes and psychological depth to the stage, instead of kings and gods.

P.title: ar-theatre.c7.text
Art & Culture: The "fourth wall" is the invisible wall between actors and audience. Brecht broke it on purpose, so viewers would think critically rather than get lost in illusion.

P.title: ar-theatre.c8.text
Art & Culture: Musicals blend songs, dialogue and dance. Broadway and London's West End host long-running shows seen by millions.

P.title: ar-theatre.c9.text
Art & Culture: After the Second World War, playwrights like Beckett wrote plays where little happens. In *Waiting for Godot*, two men wait for someone who never arrives.

P.title: ar-design.q0.o1
Art & Culture: Small strokes at the end of letters

P.title: ar-design.c0.text
Art & Culture: Serifs are small strokes at the end of letters; sans-serif fonts have none. Serifs feel traditional; sans serif feels modern and clean.

P.title: ar-design.c1.text
Art & Culture: Around 1450, Gutenberg's movable-type press made books far cheaper, spreading literacy, science and new ideas across Europe.

P.title: ar-design.c2.text
Art & Culture: Good design guides the eye: the most important thing is biggest or boldest, then the next. Without hierarchy, everything shouts at once.

P.title: ar-design.c3.text
Art & Culture: Empty space isn't wasted. It gives elements room to breathe and makes designs feel calm and premium.

P.title: ar-design.c4.text
Art & Culture: Designers use invisible grids to align elements consistently. Magazines, websites and posters all rely on them.

P.title: ar-design.c5.text
Art & Culture: A great logo is simple, memorable and works at any size, even in one colour. The best are recognisable from their shape alone.

P.title: ar-design.c6.text
Art & Culture: The Bauhaus school (1919–1933) in Germany merged art, craft and industry. "Form follows function" and clean geometric design shaped modern design.

P.title: ar-design.c7.text
Art & Culture: Mid-century Swiss designers used grids, sans-serif type and objective layouts. Helvetica (1957) came from this movement.

P.title: ar-design.c8.text
Art & Culture: For body text, around 50–75 characters per line, decent size and strong contrast make reading comfortable.

P.title: ar-design.c9.text
Art & Culture: Design isn't decoration. It solves problems: a clear road sign, an easy form, a usable app. Test with real people.

P.title: ar-colour.summary
Art & Culture: How it works and how it makes us feel.

P.title: ar-colour.q0.q
Art & Culture: Mixing red, green and blue light makes…

P.title: ar-colour.q1.q
Art & Culture: Roughly how many men have colour vision deficiency?

P.title: ar-colour.c0.text
Art & Culture: Painters' primary colours (red, yellow, blue) mix into secondaries (orange, green, purple). Colours opposite each other are complementary.

P.title: ar-colour.c1.text
Art & Culture: Light mixes additively: red, green and blue make white, as on screens. Paint mixes subtractively: cyan, magenta and yellow make dark, as in printers.

P.title: ar-colour.c2.text
Art & Culture: Hue is the colour family, saturation is its intensity and value is its lightness. Changing value often matters more than changing hue.

P.title: ar-colour.c3.text
Art & Culture: Designers combine colours using simple rules: complementary for contrast, analogous (neighbours) for calm, triadic for balance.

P.title: ar-colour.c4.text
Art & Culture: Reds, oranges and yellows feel warm and seem to come forward; blues and greens feel cool and recede.

P.title: ar-colour.c5.text
Art & Culture: Colour meanings vary: white is for weddings in much of the West but for mourning in parts of Asia. Red means luck in China and danger on road signs.

P.title: ar-colour.c5.viz.items.0.b
Art & Culture: weddings in the West, mourning in parts of Asia

P.title: ar-colour.c6.text
Art & Culture: Ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan, was once worth more than gold. Painters often reserved it for the Virgin Mary's robes.

P.title: ar-colour.c7.text
Art & Culture: About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have colour vision deficiency, usually difficulty telling red and green apart. Good design never relies on colour alone.

P.title: ar-colour.c8.text
Art & Culture: The same grey looks lighter on black and darker on white. Colours change depending on their neighbours.

P.title: ar-colour.c9.text
Art & Culture: In 1960, artist Yves Klein patented his own intense ultramarine, International Klein Blue, and painted monochrome canvases with it.

P.title: ar-pop.c0.text
Art & Culture: The blues grew from African American communities in the US South around 1900, from work songs and spirituals. Its 12-bar form underlies rock and roll.

P.title: ar-pop.c1.text
Art & Culture: Jazz, born in New Orleans in the early 1900s, emphasises improvisation and swing. Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington and Miles Davis shaped it.

P.title: ar-pop.c2.text
Art & Culture: In the 1950s, Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Elvis Presley fused blues, gospel and country. Teenagers had their own music for the first time.

P.title: ar-pop.c3.text
Art & Culture: The Beatles transformed pop between 1962 and 1970, from simple love songs to studio experiments. They remain the best-selling act in history.

P.title: ar-pop.c4.text
Art & Culture: Hip hop began in the Bronx in the 1970s with DJs looping breakbeats at block parties. It's now one of the world's most listened-to genres.

P.title: ar-pop.c5.text
Art & Culture: Synthesisers and drum machines led to disco, house, techno and EDM. Detroit and Chicago shaped techno and house in the 1980s.

P.title: ar-pop.c6.text
Art & Culture: MTV launched in 1981 with "Video Killed the Radio Star". Michael Jackson's *Thriller* (1982) became the best-selling album ever.

P.title: ar-pop.c7.text
Art & Culture: Portugal's music ranges from fado to Zeca Afonso's "Grândola, Vila Morena", signal for the 1974 revolution, to Salvador Sobral's 2017 Eurovision win.

P.title: ar-pop.c8.text
Art & Culture: Streaming now accounts for most recorded music revenue. Artists earn fractions of a cent per stream, so touring matters more than ever.

P.title: ar-pop.c9.text
Art & Culture: Earworms tend to have simple, repetitive melodies with an unexpected twist. Chewing gum or doing a puzzle can help get rid of them.

P.title: ar-dance.q0.q
Art & Culture: Which dance is from the Minho region?

P.title: ar-dance.q1.q
Art & Culture: Which dance style appeared at the Paris 2024 Olympics?

P.title: ar-dance.c0.text
Art & Culture: Every known culture dances: for celebration, worship, courtship and storytelling. Dancing releases endorphins and bonds groups.

P.title: ar-dance.c1.text
Art & Culture: Ballet began in Italian and French courts in the 15th–17th centuries. Louis XIV, a keen dancer, founded the first dance academy in 1661. French terms are still used worldwide.

P.title: ar-dance.c2.text
Art & Culture: Tchaikovsky's *Swan Lake* (1877) was a flop at first. Revived in 1895, it became the most performed ballet in the world.

P.title: ar-dance.c3.text
Art & Culture: Isadora Duncan danced barefoot and freely; Martha Graham built a technique from breathing and contraction. Modern dance rebelled against ballet's rules.

P.title: ar-dance.c4.text
Art & Culture: Tango was born in the working-class districts of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late 1800s, mixing European, African and local influences.

P.title: ar-dance.c5.text
Art & Culture: Portugal's folk dances include the vira of the Minho, the corridinho of the Algarve and the pauliteiros' stick dances of Miranda do Douro.

P.title: ar-dance.c6.text
Art & Culture: Flamenco from Andalusia combines singing, guitar, dance and handclaps, with Romani, Moorish and Andalusian roots. UNESCO-listed in 2010.

P.title: ar-dance.c7.text
Art & Culture: Breaking, locking, popping and krumping grew from streets and clubs. Breaking even debuted at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

P.title: ar-dance.c8.text
Art & Culture: Kizomba, a close partner dance from Angola, spread through Lisbon's clubs to become popular across Europe.

P.title: ar-dance.c9.text
Art & Culture: Dancing combines rhythm, memory, balance and social connection. Studies link it to better balance and wellbeing in older adults.

P.title: ar-myth.q0.q
Art & Culture: Which word comes from the god Pan?

P.title: ar-myth.q1.q
Art & Culture: Thursday is named after which god?

P.title: ar-myth.q2.q
Art & Culture: Who did the Portuguese expect to return on a foggy morning?

P.title: ar-myth.c0.text
Art & Culture: Myths explain the world, teach values and give communities shared identity. Their characters and plots still shape films, books and everyday words.

P.title: ar-myth.c1.text
Art & Culture: The Greek gods lived on Mount Olympus, led by Zeus. They were powerful but very human: jealous, vain and often quarrelling.

P.title: ar-myth.c2.text
Art & Culture: Many words come from myths: "panic" from the god Pan, "echo" from a nymph, "narcissist" from Narcissus, "Achilles' heel" from Achilles.

P.title: ar-myth.c3.text
Art & Culture: Romans adopted Greek gods under new names. Our planets carry the Roman names.

P.title: ar-myth.c4.text
Art & Culture: Norse mythology features Odin, Thor and Loki, the world tree Yggdrasil and Ragnarök, the end of the world. Our weekdays Wednesday to Friday are named after Norse gods.

P.title: ar-myth.c5.text
Art & Culture: Osiris was killed by his brother Set and brought back by Isis, becoming lord of the afterlife. The dead's hearts were weighed against a feather.

P.title: ar-myth.c6.text
Art & Culture: Almost every culture has a creation story: from chaos, from an egg, from the body of a giant, or from a word. Comparing them reveals shared human questions.

P.title: ar-myth.c7.text
Art & Culture: Flood stories appear in Mesopotamia (Gilgamesh), the Bible (Noah), Greece (Deucalion) and India (Manu). Some may echo real ancient floods.

P.title: ar-myth.c8.text
Art & Culture: Portugal has legends of mouras encantadas, enchanted Moorish maidens guarding treasures, and King Sebastião, expected to return on a foggy morning.

P.title: ar-myth.c9.text
Art & Culture: Superheroes, Star Wars and fantasy sagas borrow from myth: heroes, mentors, quests and monsters. Thor is now a Marvel character.

P.title: ar-fashion.q0.q
Art & Culture: Who popularised the little black dress?

P.title: ar-fashion.q1.q
Art & Culture: Why were trade routes called the Silk Road?

P.title: ar-fashion.q1.o1
Art & Culture: Silk was a precious traded good

P.title: ar-fashion.c0.text
Art & Culture: Clothes signal identity, status, belonging and mood. Uniforms, subcultures and dress codes all communicate without words.

P.title: ar-fashion.c1.text
Art & Culture: Silk, made in China for thousands of years, was so valuable that trade routes across Asia were named after it. Its production was a closely guarded secret.

P.title: ar-fashion.c2.text
Art & Culture: Spinning and weaving machines in 18th-century Britain made cloth cheap, transforming fashion and work, and creating harsh factory conditions.

P.title: ar-fashion.c3.text
Art & Culture: In the 1850s Charles Frederick Worth in Paris became the first designer to sign his work. Haute couture means handmade, made-to-measure fashion.

P.title: ar-fashion.c4.text
Art & Culture: Coco Chanel freed women from corsets with comfortable jersey, the little black dress (1926) and trousers. Comfort became chic.

P.title: ar-fashion.c5.text
Art & Culture: Jeans began as workwear: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented riveted denim trousers in 1873. Later, film stars made them a symbol of youth.

P.title: ar-fashion.c6.text
Art & Culture: Fast fashion copies runway trends in weeks at low prices. The industry produces large shares of global textile waste and emissions.

P.title: ar-fashion.c7.text
Art & Culture: Northern Portugal, around Guimarães, Braga and Porto, has a strong textile and shoe industry, producing for major global brands. Portuguese shoes are among Europe's most exported.

P.title: ar-fashion.c7.viz.items.0
Art & Culture: Textiles in the Vale do Ave

P.title: ar-fashion.c7.viz.items.1
Art & Culture: Shoes in Felgueiras and São João da Madeira

P.title: ar-fashion.c8.text
Art & Culture: Buying fewer, better clothes, repairing, swapping and second-hand shopping reduce fashion's footprint. The most sustainable garment is the one you already own.

P.title: ar-fashion.c9.text
Art & Culture: Check fibre content and care instructions. Natural fibres like wool and linen breathe; synthetics shed microplastics when washed.

P.title: ar-food.q0.q
Art & Culture: Which Indian dish takes its name from Portuguese "vinha d'alhos"?

P.title: ar-food.c0.text
Art & Culture: Some anthropologists argue cooking helped humans evolve big brains by making food easier to digest and release more energy.

P.title: ar-food.c1.text
Art & Culture: After 1492, crops crossed oceans: tomatoes, potatoes, chillies and maize came to Europe; wheat, sugar and coffee spread to the Americas.

P.title: ar-food.c2.text
Art & Culture: Portuguese navigators spread chillies to India, tempura to Japan and pão de ló to Japan as castella. Vindaloo comes from the Portuguese "vinha d'alhos".

P.title: ar-food.c3.text
Art & Culture: Portugal eats about 20% of the world's cod, though cod doesn't swim in Portuguese waters. Salting allowed it to keep on long voyages. Legend says there are 365 recipes, or 1,001.

P.title: ar-food.c3.viz.steps.0
Art & Culture: Cod caught in the North Atlantic

P.title: ar-food.c4.text
Art & Culture: Monks at the Jerónimos Monastery made custard tarts using leftover egg yolks, since whites were used to starch clothes. After 1834, the recipe went to a nearby bakery in Belém.

P.title: ar-food.c5.text
Art & Culture: UNESCO recognised the Mediterranean diet, including Portugal, in 2013. Olive oil, vegetables, legumes, fish and shared meals are its pillars.

P.title: ar-food.c6.text
Art & Culture: Umami, the fifth taste, was identified in 1908 by Kikunae Ikeda in Japanese dashi broth. It's the savoury taste of tomatoes, cheese and broths.

P.title: ar-food.c7.text
Art & Culture: Many cuisines rely on fermentation: cheese, bread, wine, kimchi, soy sauce. Microbes transform flavour and preserve food.

P.title: ar-food.c8.text
Art & Culture: Portugal has over 250 native grape varieties. The Douro, demarcated in 1756, produces port wine, fortified with grape spirit to stop fermentation.

P.title: ar-food.c9.text
Art & Culture: Browning toast, seared steak and roasted coffee taste rich because of the Maillard reaction between sugars and proteins at high heat.

P.title: ar-games.q1.q
Art & Culture: Which graphic novel won a Pulitzer Prize?

P.title: ar-games.c0.text
Art & Culture: Board games are ancient: Senet in Egypt, the Royal Game of Ur in Mesopotamia and Go in China, played for over 2,500 years.

P.title: ar-games.c1.text
Art & Culture: Chess emerged in India around the 6th century as chaturanga, travelled through Persia and the Arab world and reached Europe around 1000. The powerful queen appeared in the 1400s.

P.title: ar-games.c2.text
Art & Culture: From *Pong* (1972) to open-world adventures, video games became the biggest entertainment industry, larger than film and music combined.

P.title: ar-games.c3.text
Art & Culture: Games combine visuals, music, writing and interaction. Museums like MoMA now collect them, though critics once said they couldn't be art.

P.title: ar-games.c4.text
Art & Culture: Good games balance challenge and skill, give clear goals and satisfying feedback: the same ingredients as "flow" in psychology.

P.title: ar-games.c5.text
Art & Culture: Comics tell stories in sequences of images. Modern comic strips grew in newspapers in the 1890s; superhero comic books boomed from 1938.

P.title: ar-games.c6.text
Art & Culture: Japanese manga is read from right to left and covers every genre. Osamu Tezuka, creator of *Astro Boy*, shaped its style.

P.title: ar-games.c7.text
Art & Culture: Long-form comics like *Maus*, which won a Pulitzer Prize in 1992, showed comics can tackle serious history and memoir.

P.title: ar-games.c8.text
Art & Culture: The Amadora International Comics Festival, since 1990, is one of Portugal's biggest cultural events. Portuguese artists draw for major international publishers.

P.title: ar-games.c9.text
Art & Culture: Modern board games like *Catan* (1995) and cooperative games sparked a boom in tabletop gaming, with thousands of new titles each year.

P.title: ar-museums.q0.q
Art & Culture: What did Picasso's Guernica respond to?

P.title: ar-museums.q0.o1
Art & Culture: The bombing of a Basque town

P.title: ar-museums.q1.q
Art & Culture: Where is Bosch's Temptations of St Anthony?

P.title: ar-museums.q1.o1
Art & Culture: National Museum of Ancient Art, Lisbon

P.title: ar-museums.c0.text
Art & Culture: Van Gogh painted *The Starry Night* in 1889 from memory, while in an asylum in Saint-Rémy. Its swirling sky is among the most recognised images in art.

P.title: ar-museums.c1.text
Art & Culture: Velázquez's *Las Meninas* (1656) shows the painter himself at work, with the royal couple reflected in a mirror. Who is looking at whom?

P.title: ar-museums.c2.text
Art & Culture: Picasso's *Guernica* (1937) responded to the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. Its broken figures became a universal anti-war symbol.

P.title: ar-museums.c3.text
Art & Culture: Edvard Munch's *The Scream* (1893) expresses anxiety: a figure under a blood-red sky. Munch made several versions in paint and print.

P.title: ar-museums.c4.text
Art & Culture: Vermeer's painting (c. 1665) isn't a portrait but a "tronie", a study of a face. Vermeer made only about 35 known paintings.

P.title: ar-museums.c5.text
Art & Culture: Hokusai's *The Great Wave off Kanagawa* (c. 1831) is a woodblock print, made in thousands of copies. It inspired European artists like Monet and Van Gogh.

P.title: ar-museums.c6.text
Art & Culture: Hieronymus Bosch's *The Temptations of St Anthony* is in Lisbon's National Museum of Ancient Art, full of fantastical creatures.

P.title: ar-museums.c7.text
Art & Culture: Lisbon's Calouste Gulbenkian Museum holds a collector's treasures, from Egyptian art to Lalique jewellery. Gulbenkian, an oil magnate, spent his last years in Lisbon.

P.title: ar-museums.c8.text
Art & Culture: The Louvre welcomes around 9 million visitors a year, more than any other art museum. The Mona Lisa sits behind bulletproof glass.

P.title: ar-museums.c9.text
Art & Culture: Pick five works to see properly instead of rushing past hundreds. Arrive early, sit with one painting and read the label after looking.
